story.title: Rescue Operation Saves Woman Trapped for 36 Hours After Colombia Earthquake
story.summary: Emergency workers in Colombia successfully rescued a 32-year-old woman who had been trapped for 36 hours under the rubble of a collapsed building following a powerful earthquake. The rescue operation took 10 hours after the woman was located beneath concrete debris in Pereira, as crews continue to search for additional survivors from the country's strongest earthquake in a century.

event_overview.title: About Colombia Earthquake
event_overview.subject: Colombia Earthquake
event_overview.summary: The Colombia earthquake was a magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia on August 10, 2026, causing major building damage and trapping people beneath collapsed structures. Pereira, in the coffee-growing region of Risaralda, was among the affected cities, and the event prompted a continuing search-and-rescue and disaster-response operation.

facts.label: Start date
facts.value: The main earthquake struck on August 10, 2026; rescue and damage-assessment operations continued in the following days.

facts.label: Magnitude and affected area
facts.value: The earthquake was reported as magnitude 7.4 and affected western Colombia, including Pereira, Cali, Quibdó and Manizales; it was also felt in Ecuador and Panama.

facts.label: Pereira’s setting
facts.value: Pereira is the capital of Risaralda department and the largest city in Colombia’s Eje Cafetero (Coffee Axis); it is located in central-western Colombia.

facts.label: Seismic monitoring
facts.value: The Servicio Geológico Colombiano (SGC) is the national geological authority that publishes earthquake information and seismic-hazard tools; its seismic catalog contains events from 1993 onward and says entries are manually reviewed by SGC seismology analysts.

facts.label: Response framework
facts.value: Colombia’s disaster-risk system is established under Law 1523 of 2012. The law assigns disaster-risk management to national and territorial authorities and gives the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) a coordinating role across the system.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows the immediate rescue phase in Pereira on August 12-13, 2026, rather than providing a complete account of all affected places, casualty revisions, relief measures, or longer-term recovery.

explore_lenses.label: Why is this rescue significant now?
explore_lenses.title: A rare success during a narrowing rescue window
explore_lenses.summary: The rescue is significant because it came more than a day after the August 10 quake, while crews were still searching across multiple badly damaged cities. It also demonstrates why rescuers continued targeted operations despite the rapidly falling odds of finding survivors.

claims.text: Daniela Largo was pulled alive from rubble in Pereira late on August 11 after a complex rescue in which crews created an opening to free her pinned arm and a doctor gave her IV fluids.

Aid agencies regard the first 48 to 72 hours after an earthquake as crucial for recovering survivors alive, although survival can extend beyond that window when trapped people have access to water and food.
Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said rescue teams were still detecting signs of life under rubble and described the following 20 hours as critical.

explore_lenses.label: How did the disaster become so severe?
explore_lenses.title: A major quake hit dense cities and remote areas
explore_lenses.summary: The magnitude 7.4 earthquake affected western Colombia, including Pereira, Cali, Manizales and Quibdó, causing building collapses and transport disruption. Damage assessment and relief were complicated by the remoteness and weak communications around the Chocó epicentral area.

claims.text: The Colombian Geological Service characterized the August 10 earthquake as the country’s strongest recorded in the 21st century; it was followed by aftershocks.
The epicenter was near San José del Palmar in Chocó, while Pereira and other western Colombian cities sustained severe damage; the quake was also felt in Ecuador and Panama.
AP reported that Chocó’s difficult access and communications outages limited early information about damage and casualties in rural areas.

The Colombian Geological Service says its seismic-hazard tools support estimating expected ground motion and informing earthquake-resistant building design, underscoring that a quake’s impacts depend on both shaking and structural exposure.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after the rescue phase?
explore_lenses.title: Search operations give way to aid and recovery
explore_lenses.summary: Authorities were continuing searches while incoming assistance was being directed toward displaced and affected families. The immediate priorities are locating missing people, stabilizing survivors and assessing damage, followed by longer-term reconstruction.

claims.text: President Abelardo de la Espriella said on August 12 that at least 265 people had died, nearly 500 were reported missing and more than 25,800 families had been affected.
De la Espriella said the government’s efforts were focused on people still missing, while regional partners were sending aid.

Forecast: As the survival window closes, operations are likely to shift increasingly from live rescue toward body recovery, shelter, medical care and damage assessment; this is an inference from the 48-to-72-hour rescue benchmark cited by aid agencies.

story_report.summary: Rescuers in Pereira pulled a 32-year-old woman alive from earthquake rubble after she had been trapped for 36 hours, completing the operation 10 hours after locating her. The rescue offered a rare survival case as Colombia’s emergency response continued after the August 10 quake, which authorities described as the country’s strongest recorded this century. President Abelardo de la Espriella said on August 12 that at least 265 people had died, nearly 500 were missing and more than 25,800 families had been affected.

sections.heading: Daniela Largo Rescue in Pereira
sections.body: The woman rescued in Pereira was identified as Daniela Largo. Crews created an opening to free her pinned arm, while a doctor administered intravenous fluids before she was pulled from the rubble late on August 11. Aid agencies consider the first 48 to 72 hours after an earthquake crucial for finding survivors alive, though people can survive longer if they have access to water and food.

sections.heading: Earthquake Damage Across Western Colombia
sections.body: The earthquake’s epicenter was near San José del Palmar in Chocó, and it was followed by aftershocks. Pereira and other western Colombian cities sustained severe damage, while the shaking was felt in Ecuador and Panama. Early assessments in rural Chocó were constrained by difficult access and communications outages, limiting information about damage and casualties.

sections.heading: Rescue Window Narrows for Survivors
sections.body: Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said rescue teams were still detecting signs of life beneath rubble and called the following 20 hours critical. De la Espriella said the government was focused on people still missing as regional partners sent aid. Based on the 48-to-72-hour rescue benchmark cited by aid agencies, operations are likely to shift increasingly toward body recovery, shelter, medical care and damage assessment as the survival window closes.

unresolved.text: Casualty and missing-person totals remained provisional: the August 12 official count of nearly 500 missing was far below civilian-run databases cited by AP that listed more than 4,100 people.
The available reporting does not establish why particular buildings collapsed, including any specific structural or regulatory factors.
